title: interval representations, merging, and scheduling
concepts: An interval is defined by endpoints and an endpoint convention such as closed, open, or half-open; that convention determines whether touching intervals overlap.
Sorting intervals by start or end endpoint exposes an order that supports merging, selection, and greedy scheduling, but the correct key depends on the objective.
A merge scan maintains the current merged interval and extends its end only when the next interval overlaps under the chosen endpoint convention.
Insertion into an already sorted, disjoint interval list can emit earlier intervals, merge the overlap region, then append later intervals in one pass.
For maximum-cardinality non-overlapping interval scheduling, selecting the compatible interval with the earliest finishing time admits an exchange argument proving optimality.
Minimum removal to eliminate overlaps is equivalent to retaining a maximum-size compatible subset when every interval has equal removal cost.
Sorting dominates the typical O(n log n) complexity; a scan after sorting is linear, while already sorted input can permit a linear pass.
Unbounded integer endpoints, equal endpoints, empty intervals, duplicate intervals, and inclusive versus exclusive boundaries are common correctness hazards.
